fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 1 says those in attendance were watching Him closely. When a whole table has its eyes on one guest, I think something is about to happen.
Close, but it's the opposite. Leaving someone alone means they get to eat in peace, and verse 1 says those in attendance were watching Him closely. So Jesus goes to eat with eyes on Him.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” (Luke 14:3). He puts the question to the experts in the law and the Pharisees, and He puts it right out loud. A man with dropsy is right there before Him, so the question is not just a theory.

Good memory for a Bible question, but that one belongs to another scene. Some people asked Him about Caesar and taxes in Matthew 22:17. Here at the dinner, the question is about healing on the Sabbath. That's the one with a man with dropsy right there before Him.
Yes, baker. Verse 4 says Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. Nobody answered His question, and Jesus healed the man anyway. Healed is the word the verse uses.
Anointing is a real thing in Scripture, but it's not what the text says here. Verse 4 says Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. So the word that fits is healed.
Jesus does a lot of teaching at this dinner, but the text doesn't say He teaches this man. Verse 4 says He took hold of him, healed him, and sent him on his way. The word the verse uses is healed.
The host's family never shows up in this parable. Jesus says, “…do not sit in the place of honor…” (Luke 14:8). So the seat to leave alone is the place of honor.

Yes, baker. Jesus says not to sit there “…in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.” (Luke 14:8). Then verse 9 says the host will come and tell you, “Give this man your seat.” That's the risk of grabbing the place of honor.
Room isn't the problem in this parable. Verse 8 says the reason is “…in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.” The worry is about who else has been invited.

Yes, baker. Verse 9 says the host will tell you to give your seat away, and “…in humiliation, you will have to take the last place.” You started at the top and ended at the bottom. That's quite a drop.

Front isn't the word the verse uses. The host says, “Give this man your seat.” and then verse 9 says you “…will have to take the last place.” So you start in the place of honor and end in the last place.

Yes, baker. Verse 10 says that when you sit in the last place, your host may come and say, “Friend, move up to a better place.” That's the opposite of the humiliation in verse 9. This time the host is the one who tells you to move up.
Being ignored isn't what the verse says. When the host moves you up, verse 10 says you “…will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.” The whole table sees it.
No-shows aren't the reason in the text. Verse 12 says, “Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.” The worry Jesus names is that they may invite you in return.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” (Luke 14:14). Those are the guests He tells the host to invite, and they can't repay him. So the repaying comes at the resurrection of the righteous.

Yes, baker. He says, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.” (Luke 14:19). He has bought them and says he's going to try them out. Five yoke is a lot of oxen to try out on banquet day.
Selling isn't what he says. He says, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out.” (Luke 14:19). His excuse is trying them out.

Yes, baker. The owner says to bring in “…the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” (Luke 14:21). Earlier Jesus told the host to invite “…the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind…” (Luke 14:13). That's the same group Jesus named to the host.
The temple courts don't come up in the story. After the servant says there is still room, the master says, “Go out to the highways and hedges…” (Luke 14:23). That's the next place he names.
The city gates aren't named. The servant is told, “Go out to the highways and hedges…” (Luke 14:23). That's the next place the master names after the servant says there is still room.

It goes the other way. The master says, “For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.” (Luke 14:24). The men invited first are the ones who made excuses, and he says not one of them will taste his banquet.
